newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan calls for restraint after food riots.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan calls for restraint after food riots.

text.p: The Pakistani government called on Tuesday for its citizens to buy less food and not to hoard after three days of food riots and protests in two provinces sparked by a scarcity of wheat.

Food and Agriculture Minister Abida Hussain said, however, domestic stocks and shipments of imported wheat due to arrive this month would be sufficient until all the country's four provinces harvested their own new wheat crop.

She told a news conference that the situation was "under control" on Tuesday in the northwestern city of Peshawar after Monday's food riots there during which protesters looted stocks, attacked flour mills and blocked roads.
Protests were also held in other towns in the North West Frontier province, of which Peshawar is the capital, and in the southwestern province of Baluchistan.
"I would make an appeal to all to observe Islamic norms at this juncture not to buy more than necessary and not to hoard," Hussain said.
"I want to make it clear that people blocking roads, mobbing flour mills and forcing shops to close down are making the process of supply, flour production and distribution difficult."

The crisis is the first Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government has had to face, coming just six weeks after he took power following the landslide victory of his Pakistan Muslim League party in February 3 general elections.
The government blames the wheat shortage on smuggling to neighbouring countries, particularly to war-torn Afghanistan, hoarding and late arrival of imports.
Hussain said Pakistan's provincial food departments were notorious for corruption and their records had shown more wheat stocks than had actually existed.
She said the government would punish those responsible for the crisis after the new crop had been harvested.
Ahmed Mukhtar, secretary general of the opposition Pakistan People's Party (PPP) of former prime minister Benazir Bhutto, said the flour crisis was likely to continue until mid-May.
"It is the for the first time in Pakistan's history that food riots took place owing to wheat shortage," he told a news conference in Islamabad.
He said an agricultural package announced by Sharif last week raising the government's support price for wheat, the staple food of Pakistanis, would make it unaffordable for poorer citizens.
